short: Ten months of deliberate attrition that became France's defining ordeal of the war.
full:
Falkenhayn chose Verdun because the French would not give it up. The fortress city on the Meuse carried too much prestige to abandon, so an attack there would, in his account, bleed the French army white. The German bombardment opened on 21 February 1916 with more than a thousand guns. Fort Douaumont fell within four days almost without a fight, and the battle then ground on across ridges and ravines whose names — Mort-Homme, Cote 304, Fleury — passed into French memory.

Petain organised the defence around the Voie Sacree, the single road up which lorries carried men and shells day and night, and rotated divisions through it so that most of the French army served at Verdun at some point. The Germans took Fort Vaux in June and came within four miles of the city, then were pushed back through the autumn by French counterattacks. When the fighting stopped on 18 December the line was roughly where it had begun, and around 300,000 men were dead.
